title: What is known about 1RB0LC_1LC0RD_1LF1LA_1LB1RE_1RB1LE_---0LE
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LC_1LC0RD_1LF1LA_1LB1RE_1RB1LE_---0LE.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and it is a Collatz-type question. Lean proves (kernel) that the machine halts from blank tape exactly when an explicit four-counter map, started at (15, 7, 7, 1), reaches its halting case. The map has survived four ends of its budget; the budget now holds a number of pairs with 399,947 binary digits, and whether the machine halts when that runs out depends on two parities that behave like coin flips.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 25,918 cells have been visited and 25,890 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.527). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Thirty macro rules
claims.text: Between two visits of the head (state E, reading 0) to the left end of the tape, the tape E>0 1^a 0 1 0 1^b (01)^c (11101)^k 1 becomes the next one of that shape, by one of 28 rules, each proved for all values of its parameters; two more rules show the halt.

claims.title: Halts if and only if the map halts
claims.text: Iterate next from (15, 7, 7, 1), reached after 1,188 steps: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit reaches halt, the case a = 1, c = 1, b even. An invariant shows the orbit never takes the uncovered cases.

claims.title: The map agrees with the machine
claims.text: At all 16,366 visits of the head to the left end in the first 4·10<sup>8</sup> steps the tape has the predicted (a, b, c, k).

claims.title: Four budget ends survived, the fifth out of reach
claims.text: The orbit, computed exactly with whole stretches of rounds at once: the budget runs out at phases 4, 34, 683,741 and 683,742 and is refilled each time, to 59 pairs, 1,367,414 pairs, one pair borrowed from the suffix, and then a number of 399,947 bits. Spending that takes about 2<sup>399,946</sup> more phases.

claims.title: A coin flip per budget
claims.text: When the last pair is reached the machine halts if the phase ends with a = 1 (rather than 0) and b is even. If those parities behave like fair coins each budget end halts with probability about 1/4, so the machine would halt with probability 1, but only after a time beyond any computation.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Equivalent to whether the orbit of (15, 7, 7, 1) under the map ever ends a budget on the wrong parities: a Collatz-type question like Antihydra's, out of reach of current methods.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and it is a Collatz-type problem. The machine runs a counter that grows by half each phase and pays two pairs of a budget per phase; when the budget runs out it either halts or refills it, depending on parities that behave like coin flips. Lean proves that this description is exact.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: the machine is exactly the four-counter map below.
survived; the fifth budget holds a 399,947-bit number of pairs.
No halt in the C simulator; 25,918 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Two blocks, a budget and a suffix
html: Stop the machine every time the head, in state E, reads the 0 at the left end of the tape. The tape then always reads

two blocks of 1s, of lengths a and b, then a budget of c pairs 0 1, then a suffix of k words 11101. In one round the head runs to the end of the second block and back: two 1s leave the first block and three join the second, (a, b) → (a − 2, b + 3). When the first block is down to 1 or 0 cells the second block becomes the first, a new second block of 7 cells is started and two pairs are spent: (1, b, c) → (b, 7, c − 2), (0, b, c) → (b − 1, 7, c − 2) (and (2, b) first becomes (0, b + 3)).
So a phase takes the first block a to about 3a/2: (3a + 11)/2 for odd a and 3a/2 + 6 for even a, the map of Antihydra with other constants, and every phase costs two pairs.

When only one pair is left, the pairs are refilled from the second block: with a = 0 to b/2 − 3 or (b − 1)/2 pairs, with a = 1 and b odd to (b − 1)/2 pairs, and each refill adds one word 11101 to the suffix. With a = 1 and b even the machine halts. When no pair is left at all, the first word of the suffix serves as one more pair.

Lean proves each of these rules for all values (lean/Rules.lean), and from them that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if this map, started at (15, 7, 7, 1), reaches the halting case (halts_iff in lean/Map.lean).

sections.heading: A budget that runs out
html: From blank tape the budget has run out four times. At phase 4 (b = 124, refilled to 59 pairs), at phase 34 (b = 2,734,834, refilled to 1,367,414 pairs), at phase 683,741 the even budget ran out completely and a pair was taken from the suffix, and at the next phase, with a = 1 and b odd (a number of 399,948 bits), it was refilled to a number of pairs with 399,947 bits. Spending that budget takes about 2399,946 phases; no computer will get there.

Whether the machine halts at the end of that budget depends on whether the last phase ends with a = 1 or a = 0 and on the parity of b, numbers that behave like coin flips. If they do, each budget end halts with probability about 1/4 and the machine halts with probability 1, but proving anything about those parities is the same obstacle as for Antihydra and the Collatz problem.

Try the map. Each line is one phase: the first block a is spent two cells at a time (three cells join the second block each time), then the second block becomes the first and two pairs of the budget are paid. When the budget is down to its last pair the parity of b decides.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.527). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 25,918 cells (21,154 left of the start, 13 right), with a density of 1s of 0.999.

summary: Antihydra-like: a 3/2 map on one counter, paid for from a budget of 01 pairs; it halts iff a budget ends at a = 1 with b even (survived 4 budget ends; the 5th budget holds a 399,947-bit number of pairs).
